method_note:
I read the handoff text extraction in full. Evidence retrieved in this session:
- the pinned Pospischil RS and LTS NeuroML files (raw GitHub, commit 049081c3)
- NeuroML_v2.3.1.xsd
- docs.neuroml.org simulation page
- eFEL feature documentation
- Crossref metadata for every cited DOI
- Europe PMC abstracts or full text for Prescott 2008, NeuroML-DB 2023, Koch 2023, Pospischil 2008, Korngreen 2026 and Petilla 2008
- the Semantic Scholar abstract for Papadakis 2016

Citations marked title-level (Prinz 2004, Marder and Goaillard 2006, Marder and Taylor 2011, Goaillard and Marder 2021, Madeyski 2014) were verified for bibliographic metadata only, not content. Facts attributed to the 'M0 eFEL audit' or 'M0 fixture evidence' come from the verified audit files under docs/m0_evidence. No simulations were run. No result claims are made. No held-out data was created or accessed.

issues.handoff_section: Protocols (items 3-4 and 'Normalize principal depolarizing tests to model-specific rheobase'); Features (Rheobase); Protocol selection (detection matrix)
issues.assumption: Normalising depolarising protocols to model-specific rheobase makes tests comparable, and it is harmless to apply the same normalisation when testing mutants and transformed models.
issues.analysis:
The handoff does not say whether a mutant (or valid transformation) is stimulated at a multiple of the REFERENCE model's rheobase or of its OWN re-measured rheobase. If each mutant is re-normalised, the normalisation absorbs exactly the faults that shift excitability, a core biophysical fault class.

The pilot fixture RS shows this cleanly. It is a single isopotential 96 um soma segment, its conductances are densities, and its stimulus is an absolute current (pulseGenerator amplitude 7.5E-10 A in RS.net.nml). For an isopotential compartment without area-dependent concentration terms, the membrane equation depends on injected current only through current per unit area. So an area or diameter mutation, or a diameter unit error, shifts rheobase in proportion. After re-normalisation every protocol delivers the same current density, and all normalised features are unchanged apart from numerical error.

Mutations that mainly move threshold (leak conductance, Na vShift, erev) are partly absorbed the same way, leaving the rheobase feature as the only detector. Detection rates and the RQ6 fault-to-protocol attributions would then reflect the normalisation choice, not the protocols.

The protocols are also not independent columns in the binary detection matrix: protocol 4 cannot run without protocol 3 (rheobase search). Count-matched random sets that include a normalised protocol silently include an extra search protocol, and runtime-matched sets must carry its cost.
issues.recommendation:
1. Use reference-anchored stimulation in the primary analysis. Run rheobase search once per reference model under a frozen, hashed definition. Convert the rheobase multiples into absolute currents, and apply identical absolute stimuli to that reference, its valid transformations and all its mutants.
2. Measure mutant rheobase only as a separate feature, from its own search protocol.
3. Allow per-mutant re-normalisation only as a pre-registered secondary analysis.
4. Model rheobase search as an explicit prerequisite of every normalised protocol, in both the detection matrix and cost accounting.
5. Add an area-scaling mutant as a positive control, to prove the pipeline does not absorb excitability shifts.
issues.decision_question: For mutants and transformed models, should rheobase-normalised protocols use the reference model's frozen rheobase (absolute current held fixed; recommended) or each mutant's own re-measured rheobase?

issues.handoff_section: Protocols (1 zero-current baseline, 3 rheobase search, 4 fixed multiple of rheobase); Model selection ('excitability thresholds' diversity)
issues.assumption: Rheobase is a well-defined positive quantity for every intended model, found by a monotone search, and a fixed multiple of it puts different models in comparable firing regimes.
issues.analysis:
Rheobase is ill-defined or non-comparable for several model types the handoff wants.

(a) Excitability class. Prescott et al. 2008 (PLoS Comput Biol 4(10):e1000198) derive Hodgkin's three excitability classes from distinct spike-initiation dynamics and show that single-parameter changes convert a model between classes. At rheobase, defined as the minimum current eliciting at least one spike, class 2 and 3 neurons fire one short-latency spike, class 1 neurons fire slowly and repetitively, and the class 3 f-I curve is undefined. A 'fixed multiple of rheobase' therefore puts class 1 and class 2 models in qualitatively different regimes, which defeats the stated comparability goal. A mutation can also change the class, which changes what normalised features mean.

(b) Depolarisation block. Koch et al. 2023 (Front Neurol, PMC10244640) simulate single-compartment models with type I and type II firing and report one that stops firing with large current steps. Bisection with an unchecked upper bracket, and high rheobase multiples, can then fail silently.

(c) Spontaneous activity. NeuroML-DB (Birgiolas et al. 2023, PLoS Comput Biol 19(3):e1010941) reports a cluster of NeuroML cell models with non-positive rheobase that spike without stimulation. Most of its rheobase-based properties could not be computed for them, and its 1.5x/3.0x rheobase protocol also characterised rapidly adapting models poorly. For such models, 'zero-current baseline' is not a rest state and positive multiples are meaningless.

(d) Search parameters. Step duration, amplitude resolution, spike criterion and upper bound are not specified, and each changes the value. eFEL's default spike Threshold is -20 mV (M0 eFEL audit).

Bistability or hysteresis (history-dependent threshold) was not tested in this audit. It cannot be excluded for any model without an explicit ascending/descending check.
issues.recommendation:
1. Write an operational rheobase definition into the protocol manifest: step duration, amplitude bracket and maximum, bisection resolution in pA, spike criterion, a depolarisation-block check (for example eFEL depol_block_bool plus spike count at the upper bracket), and ascending plus descending sweeps to detect hysteresis.
2. Add pre-registered excitability fields to the model manifest, computed on the reference in the frozen environment: spontaneous firing at 0 nA, f-I continuity (class 1, class 2 or phasic), onset of depolarisation block, and a hysteresis flag.
3. Set an inclusion rule for non-positive-rheobase and phasic-only models. Either exclude them from the rheobase-normalised stratum, or give them a pre-registered alternative anchor, such as a holding current that silences the cell or an absolute current-density grid.
4. Stratify results by excitability class.
issues.decision_question: Should spontaneously active (non-positive rheobase) and phasic/single-spike models be excluded, or included with a separately defined, pre-registered normalisation anchor?

issues.handoff_section: Features (Voltage deflection and sag ratio); Protocols (7 hyperpolarizing step, 8 hyperpolarization-release rebound); Model selection (diversity across rebound and sag)
issues.assumption: Sag ratio and rebound are meaningful features/protocols for all models, and the planned models provide sag and rebound diversity.
issues.analysis:
Sag and rebound are mechanism-specific responses, usually attributed to hyperpolarisation-activated (Ih) and low-threshold T-type Ca currents. This attribution is general background and was not verified in this audit.

None of the pilot fixture models can express Ih-type sag, and LTS rebound is plausible but untested:
- At the pinned commit, RS.cell.nml has only Leak, Kd, IM and Na.
- LTS.cell.nml adds IT (T-type) but has no Ih.
- The M0 fixture evidence (docs/m0_evidence/fixtures/fixture_verify.json) shows no Ih in FS or IB either, and no licensed single-compartment Ih fixture was found.

This causes several problems:
- **Sag without Ih.** In models lacking these currents, sag features measure small relaxations caused by other slow currents, or come out near zero or undefined. eFEL's sag_amplitude only returns a value for a hyperpolarising deflection, and the M0 eFEL audit found that whether sag features are defined depends on the trace.
- **Near-zero tolerances.** Near zero the relative floor r|f| collapses, so the arbitrary absolute floor decides detection, and tiny numerical changes can flip a feature between defined and undefined.
- **Amplitude scaling.** Hyperpolarising and rebound amplitudes cannot be normalised by rheobase, which is a depolarising quantity, and the handoff does not say how to scale them.
- **Post-stimulus spikes.** Rebound spikes come after the stimulus ends. eFEL has no feature that counts post-stimulus spikes, and per the M0 eFEL audit its trace_check flags late spikes and mean_frequency counts only spikes inside the stimulus window.
- **Defined-to-undefined transitions.** A mutation that removes IT turns rebound features from defined to undefined, and the tolerance rule has no semantics for that transition.
- **Trivial selection.** In models without T or h currents, protocols 7 and 8 mainly detect passive changes (leak, capacitance) that other protocols also catch, so greedy selection results would reflect the model mix.
issues.recommendation:
1. Before any mutant exists, freeze a per-reference-model applicability matrix (feature x protocol). Base it on the reference's own simulated response at all refinement levels, never on mutants. For example: sag features apply only if the reference sag exceeds a pre-set absolute floor; rebound features apply only if the reference shows post-release depolarisation above a floor.
2. Scale hyperpolarising amplitudes to a target steady-state deflection in mV, or via reference input resistance.
3. Define a separate post-release analysis window for rebound, passed to eFEL with its own stim_start/stim_end.
4. Use three-state outcomes: defined-in-reference but undefined-in-mutant (or the reverse) counts as a detection, and 'not applicable' features are never compared.
5. Drop 'sag' from the pilot diversity claim unless an Ih-containing model is added.
issues.decision_question: Must the full study include at least one model with an Ih-type current (possibly needing a multicompartment/NEURON model or a separately licensed source), or should 'sag' be removed from the stated behavioural-diversity target?

issues.handoff_section: Mutations (Biophysical: 'wrong segment group'; Numerical: 'spatial discretization'); Solo scope (pilot 'jNeuroML only'; begin with single-compartment models); Leakage prevention (hold out an entire mutation family)
issues.assumption: 'Wrong segment group' and 'spatial discretization' operators yield meaningful admissible mutants in the planned models.
issues.analysis:
In single-compartment pilot models these operators cannot produce informative mutants:
- RS.cell.nml has a single segment (id 0). Its three segment groups (Soma, all, soma_group) all resolve to that one segment.
- In NeuroML_v2.3.1.xsd the channel-density segmentGroup attribute is optional, with default 'all'.
- NeuroML documentation says jLEMS simulates single-compartment models and that multicompartmental cells need NEURON.

So each operator has only degenerate outcomes:
- Re-targeting a channel density to another existing group is equivalent by construction.
- Re-targeting to a non-existent group gives a structurally invalid or non-executable mutant.
- Spatial discretisation has nothing to act on in one isopotential compartment.

These operators would only inflate the 'equivalent' and 'invalid/crash' bins of the validation cascade. That distorts RQ1 proportions and could falsely trigger the pivot rule 'most faults merely crash'.

In the full study only a few multicompartment models (run with NEURON) can exercise these operators. If either becomes the held-out mutation family, generalisation is confounded with model type and simulator.
issues.recommendation:
1. Run a static applicability check before generating mutants. The segment-group operator requires at least two segment groups with different membership and a density whose group assignment matters. Spatial discretisation requires a multicompartment cell and a simulator that uses it.
2. Record failing operators as 'not applicable', outside every cascade denominator. Do not generate equivalent-by-construction mutants and count them as 'behaviourally equivalent'.
3. Exclude both operators from the pilot.
4. Do not choose a multicompartment-only family as the held-out family unless multicompartment models exist in both the discovery and held-out splits.
issues.decision_question: Should 'wrong segment group' and 'spatial discretization' be removed from the pilot and from the operator pool for single-compartment models, and be barred as the held-out family unless both splits contain enough multicompartment models?

issues.handoff_section: Definitions (Admissible non-equivalent mutant; Empirical semantic certificate); Mutations (classification; main denominator); Mandatory rules ('Do not treat every parameter change as a defect'); Research questions 1-2, 6
issues.assumption: Whether a parameter change is a defect can be decided by whether it produces reproducible behavioural divergence somewhere in the predefined exhaustive battery.
issues.analysis:
The handoff says not every parameter change is a defect, but it gives no criterion. The only admissibility test is divergence in the exhaustive candidate battery, which makes the design circular.

(1) The battery is both the oracle and the thing being evaluated. Admissible mutants are, by definition, those detected by the union of the candidate protocols, so the exhaustive battery scores 100% by construction. Mutants that change behaviour only under stimuli outside the candidate pool are silently excluded instead of counted as misses. This inflates every battery's apparent detection rate and makes the RQ1 silent-drift rates conditional on the battery.

(2) 'Behaviourally equivalent' therefore only means 'not distinguished by this battery at this tolerance'. That is the classic equivalent-mutant problem (Madeyski et al., IEEE TSE 40(1), 2014; title-level evidence only).

(3) Deterministic simulators are extremely sensitive, so almost any conductance change will exceed numerical-refinement noise. The admissible set is then decided mainly by mutation magnitude and the arbitrary floors, not by any notion of fault.

(4) Neuroscience degeneracy means a parameter change may be a legitimate alternative rather than a fault, and fault-family attribution (RQ6) may not be identifiable from features:
- Prinz, Bucher and Marder 2004 (Nat Neurosci 7:1345), Marder and Goaillard 2006 (Nat Rev Neurosci 7:563), Marder and Taylor 2011 (Nat Neurosci 14:133) and Goaillard and Marder 2021 (Annu Rev Neurosci 44:335) describe this literature; I verified their Crossref titles only.
- Korngreen 2026 (PLoS Comput Biol 22(6):e1014458) reports that the canonical 1952 HH parameter set is one member of a heterogeneous ensemble of behaviours.
- Prescott et al. 2008 found that several parameters, each varied alone, had functionally equivalent effects on excitability.

(5) Mutants of the same parameter at several magnitudes subsume one another. Papadakis et al. (ISSTA 2016) found that mixing subsuming and subsumed mutants caused Type I errors in about 62% of arbitrary experiments lacking countermeasures.
issues.recommendation:
1. Define a fault by specification, independent of the outcome. The frozen reference file is the specification, and every mutant is an unauthorised deviation from it, recorded in the manifest with its magnitude. This matches the agent task 'change one conductance without unauthorized edits'.
2. Fix mutation magnitudes in advance on a declared grid (for example, relative factors per parameter type). Report detection as dose-response curves rather than one pooled rate.
3. Report detection rates both unconditionally (over all valid, executable mutants) and over battery-admissible mutants, labelled explicitly as battery-conditional.
4. Add an independent oracle battery with stimuli outside the candidate pool, such as a dense amplitude grid or frozen noise. Use it only to label mutants, never for selection. It bounds how many mutants were excluded only because no candidate protocol could see them.
5. Report per-parameter (subsumption-reduced) results alongside per-mutant results.
6. Rename 'behaviourally equivalent' to 'not distinguished by battery B at tolerance tau'.
issues.decision_question: Should admissibility be redefined as specification deviation with a priori magnitudes, reporting both unconditional and battery-conditional detection rates, with an independent oracle battery (stimuli outside the candidate pool) used to label mutants?

issues.handoff_section: Protocols (1 zero-current baseline; all timed protocols); Mutations (Biophysical: initial voltage; Stimulus: onset, total time); Features (baseline and steady-state voltage)
issues.assumption: Reference models start from a stable rest state, so baseline features, onset mutations and initial-voltage mutations have unambiguous meaning.
issues.analysis:
The fixtures start from an imposed initMembPotential and apply the stimulus after a fixed delay:
- RS: initMembPotential -70 mV (leak reversal -70 mV), stimulus delay 300 ms, 1000 ms simulation (LEMS_RS.xml).
- LTS: initMembPotential -84 mV (leak reversal -85 mV), stimulus delay 400 ms.

Both models contain slow processes: M-current in both, plus T-type inactivation and a Ca pool in LTS. Whether they have settled by stimulus onset is unverified. If they have not, eFEL baseline features, which average over a window just before stimulus onset, measure drift rather than rest. An onset mutation then also shifts the stimulus relative to the unfinished relaxation, mixing the intended fault with settling.

The effect of an initial-voltage mutant depends on the model's dynamics:
- In a monostable model the perturbation decays, so whether it counts as 'detected' depends only on whether some analysis window overlaps the transient. That is an artefact of window choice.
- In a bistable model it can select a different attractor.
- In a spontaneously firing model it shifts spike phase, and so first-spike latency relative to stimulus onset. NeuroML-DB reports NeuroML cell models that spike without stimulation, so this case is realistic.

The handoff defines no settling criterion and no window rule.
issues.recommendation:
1. Add a pre-registered settling check to reference acceptance: a long zero-current run in which dV/dt and all state variables stay under frozen drift thresholds before the first stimulus onset.
2. Use one common pre-stimulus settling period, at least that long, in every protocol.
3. Test for bistability during reference calibration by starting runs from at least two initial voltages.
4. Pre-register which analysis windows count for initial-voltage mutants. Report these mutants separately as transient-sensitivity mutants, not pooled with persistent biophysical faults.
5. Choose onset-mutation offsets that are exact multiples of every refinement dt.

issues.handoff_section: Model selection; Solo scope (full study: 12-16 reference models, 8-10 discovery, 4-6 held-out; begin with single-compartment models); Statistics (clustering by base model)
issues.assumption: Enough independent, openly licensed, jNeuroML-runnable single-compartment conductance-based NeuroML v2 models exist, covering tonic, adapting, bursting, rebound, sag and varied excitability, so that held-out models test generalisation meaningfully.
issues.analysis:
The M0 fixture search gives little support for this assumption.

What the search found:
- The best licensed single-compartment candidates are four cells (RS, FS, IB, LTS) from one OSB conversion of Pospischil et al. 2008 (Biol Cybern 99:427), and they share channel files. That paper's abstract describes minimal HH-type models fitted to four electrophysiological classes, with substantial variability between cells within a class.
- The other candidates were a textbook HH example and Wang-Buzsaki 1996, both tonic spikers.
- No licensed Ih model was found. The ModelDB mirror repositories for Ih and T-current models had no license. The Allen GLIF conversions are integrate-and-fire.

Wider sources are only partly usable:
- NeuroML-DB holds over 1,500 models and characterised 1,222 cell models. Its clusters include non-positive-rheobase, rapidly adapting and abstract spikers, which its standard protocol handled poorly. Per-model licenses were not examined.
- The NeuroML v2.3.1 schema includes abstract cell types (izhikevich2007Cell, adExIaFCell, hindmarshRose1984Cell, pinskyRinzelCA3Cell, fitzHughNagumo1969Cell). These can supply bursting or adaptation cheaply, but they lack channel densities, reversal potentials and gating time constants, so biophysical mutation families barely apply.
- jLEMS is documented only for single-compartment models.

Consequences:
- Reaching 12-16 models plausibly requires multicompartment models (with NEURON), abstract models, or several cells from one source paper.
- Held-out models that share channel files or a source paper with discovery models are not independent, which weakens the generalisation claim (RQ4).
- Clustering by 'base model' then understates the dependence.
- With only 4-6 held-out clusters, confidence intervals will be very wide.
issues.recommendation:
1. Before M1 freezes scope, run a feasibility census of OSB, NeuroML-DB and the NeuroML2 examples. For each model record the license, compartment count, jLEMS runnability, firing regime verified by simulation (not by paper label), channel-file lineage and source paper.
2. Treat source publication and shared channel lineage as the independence unit. Split and cluster at that level, so that no held-out model shares channel files with a discovery model.
3. Pre-register a minimum-count trigger. If fewer than N independent licensed models exist, narrow the generalisation claim or admit multicompartment/NEURON models.
4. Decide explicitly whether to include abstract cell types, as a separate stratum with its own applicable mutation families.
issues.decision_question: If the census finds fewer than about 12 independent, licensed, jLEMS-runnable conductance-based models, which fallback do you approve: (a) fewer models with a narrower generalisation claim, (b) add multicompartment models via NEURON, (c) add abstract NeuroML cell types as a separate stratum, or (d) allow multiple cells per source paper with clustering at paper level?

issues.handoff_section: Features ('Qualitative firing regime'; 'Burst count'); Model selection ('Seek diversity across tonic spiking, adaptation, bursting, rebound, sag'; record 'expected behavior'); Figures 7; Success criteria ('Interpretable feature or firing-regime changes')
issues.assumption: Firing-regime labels (tonic, adapting, bursting, rebound) are well-defined, stimulus-independent model properties that can be recorded as 'expected behavior' and compared with the numeric tolerance rule.
issues.analysis:
The handoff never defines the regime labels, and eFEL has no regime classifier. The M0 eFEL audit also found that its two burst-count variants disagreed on the same adapting train.

Paper names are not verified behaviour. The fixture called 'IB' (intrinsically bursting) has an unverified bursting label, and its reference stimulus runs past the end of the simulation.

Regime also depends on stimulus intensity. Prescott et al. 2008 show a model that fires one spike at rheobase and fires repetitively under stronger stimulation. A 'regime' therefore belongs to a model-and-protocol-amplitude pair, not to a model.

A categorical label cannot go through the rule max(tau_abs, r|f|, c|f_h - f_h/2|), because the difference between categories under refinement is not a magnitude.

Existing vocabularies are a better starting point than ad hoc labels. The Petilla terminology (Ascoli et al. 2008, Nat Rev Neurosci 9:557) is a community nomenclature for interneuron features, including physiological ones. NeuroML-DB derived data-driven clusters of NeuroML models. The specific Petilla firing-pattern terms were not read in this audit.
issues.recommendation:
1. Define regime as a deterministic rule set over frozen eFEL features, evaluated per protocol and amplitude. Fix its thresholds on discovery reference models only.
2. Align label names with Petilla physiological terms where applicable, after verifying those terms in the paper body.
3. Record 'expected behavior' in the model manifest as the rule output from simulation in the frozen environment, alongside the source paper's class name (not replacing it).
4. Treat a regime change as a separate categorical detection. Require the label to differ at h, h/2 and h/4, and to be stable under a small amplitude jitter of the reference.

issues.handoff_section: IEEE pathway ('biological interpretation'); Research question 6; Figures 7 (interpretable neuroscience case studies); Success criteria; Neel's required knowledge item 4; Final decision rule
issues.assumption: Behavioural differences detected between a reference model and its mutants support biological interpretation (e.g. which protocols reveal which kinds of neuronal faults).
issues.analysis:
NeuroSem measures whether one simulated model behaves like another under simulated stimuli. That is behaviour preservation relative to a reference. It is not biological validity (model versus real neurons), and it is not evidence about neuronal biology.

Three issues follow.

1. Tolerances come from numerical refinement, not experimental variability. A 'detected' difference can be far below cell-to-cell variation: Pospischil et al. 2008 report substantial within-class variability, and Korngreen 2026 frames the HH model as an ensemble of behaviours. Conversely, a preserved fingerprint says nothing about whether the reference itself is biologically right.

2. Fault-family-to-protocol associations depend on the model set, mutation magnitudes and tolerance floors. Koch et al. 2023 show that the same channel-property change has neuron-type-dependent firing outcomes across single-compartment models, and Prescott et al. 2008 show different parameters with functionally equivalent effects. Such associations may not transfer beyond the chosen models.

3. Reference data reused from OSB tests (.mep files) are simulated outputs, not recordings.

The handoff already warns against unsupported biological claims and lists the distinction for Neel. But its TCBB rationale asks for 'biological interpretation', which pushes the other way, and reviewers are likely to challenge any biological framing.
issues.recommendation:
1. Add a claim taxonomy to REQUIREMENTS.md and the manuscript plan:
   (i) numerical-convergence claims
   (ii) behaviour-preservation claims relative to a frozen reference
   (iii) biological-relevance claims
   Only (i) and (ii) are in scope.
2. Limit 'interpretable case studies' to within-model mechanism, e.g. which current's gating explains a detected feature change. Confirm each explanation by in-silico ablation or clamping of that current, and make no statements about real neurons.
3. Optionally, express detected differences in physiological units. Where a published experimental variability exists for the source cell class, show it only as secondary context, never as a detection threshold.
issues.decision_question: Do you accept that 'biological interpretation' in the paper is limited to within-model mechanistic explanation verified by in-silico ablation, with no claims about real neurons, even though this may weaken the TCBB-fit rationale?

issues.handoff_section: Mutations (Stimulus family: amplitude, onset, duration, total time, recorded variable; Numerical: output sampling); Protocols; Definitions (Reference model; Canonical protocol)
issues.assumption: Stimulus-family mutants are model faults that NeuroSem's protocol battery can detect, and NeuroSem can run its own protocols on a reference model without changing anything else about how that model is simulated.
issues.analysis:
In the OSB fixtures, the stimulus and other behaviour-relevant settings sit outside the cell file:
- The step (pulseGenerator 7.5E-10 A, delay 0.3 s, duration 0.4 s) and the temperature (networkWithTemperature, 36 degC) are in RS.net.nml.
- Duration, dt and the recorded quantity are in LEMS_RS.xml.
- Per the M0 fixture evidence, the LTS IT gate is temperature-scaled (q10 3 at 24 degC).

NeuroSem protocols inject their own current, which creates three problems.

(1) Stimulus mutants cannot reach the battery. If NeuroSem builds its own LEMS/network wrapper around the cell, mutations to the original net or LEMS files are invisible to every NeuroSem protocol, because the cell is unchanged. Such a mutant is detectable only by a canonical test that uses the original file. It is equivalent by construction for the battery, and it trivially favours canonical testing.

(2) The embedded stimulus contaminates the battery. If NeuroSem instead reuses the original network, the embedded 0.75 nA pulse adds to every NeuroSem stimulus unless it is removed, and removing it is itself a transformation.

(3) Harness errors are hidden from the controls. If the wrapper drops or changes temperature, integration settings or initial state, the reference and all mutants are simulated wrongly in the same way. The no-change and valid-transformation controls cannot see this, because both arms share the harness.

The 'recorded variable' and 'output sampling' mutants run into the same model/harness boundary problem.
issues.recommendation:
1. For each mutation family, state which artefact it targets (cell file, network file, LEMS simulation file, or NeuroSem protocol manifest). Score each family only against tests that actually consume that artefact.
2. Reframe stimulus-family mutants as faults in the test specification. Evaluate them against the canonical test and a NeuroSem re-implementation of it, or drop them from the model-detection denominator.
3. Add a harness-fidelity gate: accept a reference model only after the NeuroSem wrapper reproduces the model's own published or OMV reference output within tolerance. This catches temperature, dt, initial-state and stimulus-removal errors.
4. Record network-level settings (temperature, populations, removed inputs) in run provenance.
issues.decision_question: Should the stimulus mutation family be reclassified as test-specification faults (scored separately and excluded from the main model-detection denominator), or replaced as one of the pilot's three families?

issues.handoff_section: Protocols (2 weak depolarizing step, 4 fixed multiple of rheobase, 9 short suprathreshold pulse, 10 paired pulses); Tolerances (tau rule using |f_h - f_h/2|); Features (spike count, first-spike latency, ISIs, adaptation index)
issues.assumption: The numerical-refinement tolerance rule yields meaningful detection thresholds for all feature-protocol pairs, including near-threshold protocols and count-valued features.
issues.analysis:
Near rheobase, spike-based features are discontinuous or badly conditioned:
- Spike count jumps in integer steps.
- ISIs are undefined when the rheobasic response is a single spike. Prescott et al. 2008 report exactly this for class 2 and 3 models: one short-latency spike, versus slow repetitive firing in class 1.
- In class 1 near threshold, latency and ISI change steeply with tiny changes in current or parameters.

This biases detection and selection:
- Weak steps, low rheobase multiples, and short or paired pulses near threshold will 'detect' almost any mutation because they sit close to a threshold. Greedy maximum coverage will prefer them.
- Those detections are real in the model but uninformative, and they make selected batteries fragile under small amplitude changes. That threatens held-out generalisation.

The tolerance rule also has limits:
- The refinement term c|f_h - f_h/2| bounds discretisation error only when h and h/2 are in the asymptotic convergence regime.
- It says nothing useful for count-valued features.

Other work supports treating sensitivity as regime-specific:
- Korngreen 2026 reports that during spiking, parameter influence is strongly time-dependent and dominated by interactions.
- NeuroML-DB characterises NeuroML models with steps at 1.5x and 3.0x rheobase, i.e. with a margin above threshold.
issues.recommendation:
1. Pre-register amplitude margins, fixed on discovery models. Suprathreshold protocols sit at least a margin above rheobase; NeuroML-DB practice suggests 1.5x, but the exact value is to be decided. 'Weak' subthreshold steps stay at or below a fixed fraction of rheobase.
2. Detect count features with a separate rule: an integer difference must be present at h, h/2 and h/4.
3. Apply the refinement term only after observing convergence, e.g. |f_h/2 - f_h/4| < |f_h - f_h/2|. Otherwise flag that model-protocol-feature cell as numerically unreliable and exclude it from selection.
4. Add a reference amplitude-jitter control. On the unmutated reference, any feature that changes beyond tolerance under a small (e.g. +/-1%) stimulus amplitude change is marked threshold-sensitive and not used as a detector.

issues.handoff_section: Solo scope (pilot success criterion); Milestone M6 (Pilot decision); Research question 1; Definitions (Silent semantic drift; Canonical protocol)
issues.assumption: Finding at least one reproducible non-equivalent mutation that passes canonical testing but is detected elsewhere is informative evidence for proceeding past the pilot.
issues.analysis:
Silent drift of this kind is expected from basic biophysics. A voltage-dependent current is only exercised within the voltage range and timescale that the canonical protocol visits. Whether a conductance or gating mutation passes canonical testing is therefore largely decided by which canonical protocol is chosen.

In the fixtures the canonical tests are single depolarising steps:
- RS: 0.75 nA from -70 mV.
- LTS: 0.15 nA from -84 mV. Per the M0 fixture evidence, the reference spikes align with Ca transients, so IT is engaged.

In another model or at a different holding level, the same channel could be silent under the canonical step and visible only under hyperpolarising or rebound protocols. A one-example gate can therefore be passed 'by construction', and reviewers may call the phenomenon trivial.

The interesting contribution is quantitative: how often silent drift occurs, how compact a battery detects it, and whether that generalises. As written, the pilot gate cannot tell a genuine finding from a consequence of the canonical-protocol choice.
issues.recommendation:
1. Before running pilot mutants, pre-register a mechanistic prediction for each: whether it is expected to be silent under canonical testing, and why.
2. Treat predicted silent drift as a pipeline positive control, not as pilot evidence.
3. Strengthen the M6 gate: require silent drift in more than one mutation family and more than one model, including cases not predicted by construction.
4. Report silent-drift rates under at least two pre-specified canonical-protocol definitions (e.g. the model's own OSB/OMV step, and a NeuroSem standard step at a fixed rheobase multiple) to show how sensitive RQ1 is to that choice.
issues.decision_question: Should the M6 pilot gate be strengthened to require pre-registered mechanistic predictions, use predicted cases only as positive controls, and require silent drift across more than one family and model (including cases not predicted by construction)?
